plan.contextChunk:
property: conditional on $x_2$, variable $x_3$ is independent of
variable $x_1$. The joint probability of all the variables shown here is
$p(x_1, x_2, x_3, y_1, y_2, y_3) =  \phi_{12}(x_1, x_2)  \phi_{23}(x_2, x_3)
\psi_{1}(y_1, x_1) \psi_{2}(y_2, x_2) \psi_{3}(y_3, x_3)$. Using
$p(a,b) = p(a \bigm | b) p(b)$, we can also write the probability of the
$x$ variables conditioned on the observations $y$,
$$p(x_1, x_2, x_3 \bigm | y_1, y_2, y_3) =  
\frac{1}{p(\mathbf{y})} \phi_{12}(x_1, x_2)  \phi_{23}(x_2, x_3) \psi_{1}(y_1, x_1) \psi_{2}(y_2, x_2) \psi_{3}(y_3, x_3).$$
For brevity, we write $p(\mathbf{y})$ for $p(y_1, y_2, y_3)$. Thus, to
form the conditional distribution, within a normalization factor, we
simply include the observed variable values into the joint probability.
For vision applications, we often use such Markov chain structures to
describe events over time.

To capture relationships over space, a two-dimensional (2D) structure is
useful, called a **Markov random field** (MRF) @Blake2011:

![Two-dimensional Markov random field.](figures/graphical_models/mrf.png){width="48%" #fig-leafs}

Then the joint probability over all the variables factorizes into this
product: 

$$p(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{y}) = 
\frac{1}{p(\mathbf{y})}
\prod_{(i,j)} \phi_{ij}(x_i, x_j) \prod_i \psi_i(x_i, y_i),$$
where the first product is over all spatial neighbors $i$ and $j$, and the second
product is over all nodes $i$.

An example of how Markov random field models are applied to images is
depicted in @fig-leafs, which show a small image region and its context
in the image (@fig-leafs [a]). @fig-leafs [b] shows an MRF with each
node corresponding to a pixel of the image region. The states of an MRF
can be indicator variables of image segment membership for each pixel.
The states of a hypothetical most-probable configuration of this MRF are
shown as the color of each node in this illustration.

:::{#fig-leafs layout-ncol="2"}
![](figures/graphical_models/leaf2.jpg){width=97% #fig-leafs-a}

![](figures/graphical_models/leaf1.jpg){width=100% #fig-leafs-b}

Fig (a) Image to be segmented and a local region of (a) marked in red.  (b) Visualization of an MRF of nodes corresponding to image pixels inside the marked region, with states indicating segment membership, for a hypothetical most probable configuration.
::: 

## Directed Graphical Models

In addition to undirected graphical models, another type of graphical
model is commonly used. **Directed graphical models** @Koller2009
describe factorizations of the joint probability into products of
conditional probability distributions. Each node in a directed graph
contributes a well-specified factor in the joint probability: the
probability of its variable, conditioned on all the variables originating
arrows pointing into it. So this graph

![A directed graphical model with three variables.](figures/graphical_models/directed.png){width="20%" #eq-directedjoint}

denotes the joint probability,

elements: 3x3 latent grid nodes (x_ij, represented as spheres initially white)
3x3 observed nodes (y_ij, represented as spheres positioned vertically above x_ij)
Vertical line segments connecting each x_ij to its corresponding y_ij
Horizontal grid lines connecting adjacent x_ij nodes along the row direction
Depth grid lines connecting adjacent x_ij nodes along the column direction
Extended boundary lines on the right and front edges of the x-grid to indicate an infinite/larger MRF
Text labels for the back-row nodes: x_1, x_2, x_3 and y_1, y_2, y_3

interactions.label: Spatial coupling (phi)
interactions.teaches: Higher coupling forces neighboring hidden states to agree, smoothing out local noise in the observations.

interactions.label: Toggle Observation State
interactions.teaches: Clicking any top-layer observation node 'y' toggles its state (color), triggering real-time inference that propagates to the hidden 'x' nodes.

demo_steps.title: The MRF Structure
demo_steps.narration: In this 2D Markov Random Field, the bottom layer contains the hidden states (x, white), and the top layer contains our noisy observations (y, grey). Vertical edges represent local evidence (unary potentials), while the grid lines represent spatial interactions (pairwise potentials).

demo_steps.title: Independent Decisions (No Coupling)
demo_steps.narration: With spatial coupling set to 0, each hidden node 'x' is determined entirely by its own observation 'y'. If the observations are noisy (mixed colors), the estimated hidden state is equally noisy and lacks spatial coherence.

demo_steps.title: Enforcing Spatial Consistency
demo_steps.narration: Increase the coupling parameter. Now, neighboring hidden nodes penalize sudden changes. The grid performs joint inference: isolated noisy observations are smoothed out, forcing the hidden layer to form clean, continuous segments.

demo_steps.title: Interactive Belief Propagation
demo_steps.narration: Try clicking on any of the top-layer observation nodes (y) to change their values. Watch how the change dynamically propagates to its neighbors in the hidden layer (x) based on the coupling strength.

interactionPlan.camera_suggestion: An orthographic view from a slightly elevated, angled perspective looking down at the 3x3 grid, showing clear separation between the top (y) and bottom (x) layers.
interactionPlan.view_reasoning: (1) The dominant vertical lines linking x and y run straight up-and-down on the screen. The grid plane of x nodes lies flat, with grid lines running left-right and receding diagonally into the background. (2) This receding diagonal depth implies the camera is rotated around the vertical Y-axis by about -35 degrees (azimuth) to reveal the 2D grid structure clearly without alignment overlap. (3) The vertical separation between the two layers is highly visible, meaning the elevation must be high enough to see the grid rows but shallow enough to emphasize the vertical vertical edges, indicating an elevation of about 25 degrees.

camera_view.view_notes: Maintains the classic oblique textbook perspective of the graphical model where nodes align nicely along diagonal grid axes.

inline_constraints.default_view: Must match the original node positioning, horizontal layout, and vertical projection.
inline_constraints.visible_ui: A single compact slider for spatial coupling placed near the bottom edge.
inline_constraints.explainers: Clicking a top node shows a hover tooltip: 'Observed State (Click to toggle)'.
inline_constraints.framing: Keep a moderate margin around the grid to prevent boundary lines from being clipped.
inline_constraints.camera: Match the visual proportions of the original diagram exactly on first load.

interactionPlan.notes: Represent node states using distinct colors (e.g., Purple and Green representing two classes in binary segmentation). When the user toggles a 'y' node or adjusts the slider, run a quick iterative energy minimization (or basic belief propagation) step on a 3x3 MRF to update the colors of the 'x' nodes instantly. Render connection lines as simple cylinder/line elements.

evaluation.geometry_accuracy_analysis: The 3D grid topology is well preserved with two layers of 3x3 nodes connected by vertical and horizontal cylinders. Real 3D primitives are used throughout. However, the camera azimuth is rotated relative to the source, causing the depth order and left-to-right labeling ($y_1, y_2, y_3$) to be reversed or misaligned.
evaluation.geometry_accuracy_improvement: Adjust the camera azimuth angle in setCameraView to match the perspective angle of the source, restoring the correct left-to-right layout of the labeled nodes.
evaluation.interactivity_usability_analysis: The developer built three distinct functional interactions: (1) A 'φ coupling' spatial smoothness slider that alters the pairwise weight and triggers real-time MAP inference on the hidden grid; (2) Clickable 3D observation nodes (y_i) which toggle binary states and update the hidden layer immediately; (3) A 'toggle y' button in the HTML UI to toggle the selected observation. A guided step-through demo with 4 steps is implemented in the code, but it lacks dedicated UI navigation buttons (Next/Prev) and instead relies on the user clicking the background grid lines to advance, which is highly unintuitive.
evaluation.interactivity_usability_improvement: Add explicit 'Next Step' and 'Previous Step' buttons to the HTML UI to make the guided demo steps easily navigable, rather than binding step progression to clicking the grid wireframes.
evaluation.faithfulness_analysis: The overall grid topology is recognizable. However, the color scheme is incorrect: all spheres are rendered in solid black, whereas the original utilizes white for the bottom grid and gray for the top. Label positioning is also poor, causing overlapping and illegibility.
discrepancies: All nodes are rendered as solid black spheres instead of white (bottom) and gray (top) circles.
Labels overlap directly with the black spheres, making them hard to read.
Grid connecting lines are light gray rather than sharp black.
evaluation.faithfulness_improvement: Change the bottom nodes to white with black borders, top nodes to gray, and adjust label offsets to prevent overlapping with the geometry.
evaluation.label_quality_analysis: The source figure contains labels 'y1', 'y2', 'y3' and 'x1', 'x2', 'x3'. In the output, 'y1', 'y2', and 'y3' are present but out of order/disoriented relative to the original perspective. The 'x' labels lack subscripts (appearing just as 'x') and are heavily occluded by the dark, oversized node geometry.
evaluation.label_quality_improvement: Add proper subscripts to the 'x' labels, increase their offset to prevent overlap with the nodes, and ensure the 'y' labels match the original left-to-right indexing order.
evaluation.concept_accuracy_analysis: Core concept: 2D Markov Random Fields (MRFs) for spatial modeling. User-visible claims: (1) 'φ coupling' slider controls spatial coupling — accurate, it directly updates the pairwise potential weights in the energy minimization. (2) Clicking top-layer 'y' nodes toggles their observed state and recomputes the hidden states — accurate, representing real-time MAP inference under different evidence scenarios. (3) Narration steps explain that at φ = 0, decisions are independent, whereas higher φ values enforce spatial consistency — accurate and directly supports the textbook's description of Potts/MRF models. No conceptual errors or misleading claims are present.
evaluation.notes: The 3D MRF grid topology and interactive MAP inference are conceptually robust, but the visualization suffers from severe visual styling issues and camera misalignment. The nodes are rendered as solid black spheres rather than white and gray, the camera azimuth is reversed (disorienting the left-to-right order), and the labels lack subscripts and are heavily occluded by geometry.
action_items: Adjust the camera azimuth in setCameraView so the grid aligns with the source perspective, ensuring column 1 is on the left and column 3 is on the right.
Change the hidden layer node material to white with black outlines, and the observation layer node material to gray with black outlines, rather than solid black.
Fix the labels to use proper subscripts (e.g., x1, x2, x3) and increase their spatial offset from the spheres to prevent occlusion and overlapping.
Make the grid and vertical connecting cylinders solid black to match the source drawing.
Add explicit 'Next Step' and 'Previous Step' buttons to the HTML UI to let users easily navigate through the guided demo steps.

evaluation.geometry_accuracy_improvement: Reduce the radius of the black outline spheres or use a 2D ring/torus for the outline to prevent it from completely obscuring the colored inner spheres.
evaluation.interactivity_usability_analysis: The developer implemented several high-quality, functional interactions: (1) A compact slider ('spatialSmoothness') that updates the spatial coupling parameter φ in real-time, executing an exact energy-minimization MAP inference step over the 9 nodes. (2) Interactive 3D clicking on the top-layer observation nodes ('y') which toggles their states, triggering propagation. (3) A 'toggle y' button acting on the selected observation. (4) A guided step-through system ('goToStep' and 'demoSteps') that can be cycled by clicking on the grid lines, modifying coupling and explaining MRF concepts sequentially.
evaluation.faithfulness_analysis: The overall 3D grid layout and node connections successfully mimic the original graphical structure. However, the color scheme is incorrect: all nodes are rendered as solid black spheres, whereas the source features white bottom nodes and gray top nodes. This color issue also severely impacts label legibility.

evaluation.label_quality_improvement: Add a contrasting background or offset to the text labels, or change the node colors to white/grey as in the source, to prevent dark text from overlapping black spheres.

plan.contextChunk:
property: conditional on $x_2$, variable $x_3$ is independent of
variable $x_1$. The joint probability of all the variables shown here is
$p(x_1, x_2, x_3, y_1, y_2, y_3) =  \phi_{12}(x_1, x_2)  \phi_{23}(x_2, x_3)
\psi_{1}(y_1, x_1) \psi_{2}(y_2, x_2) \psi_{3}(y_3, x_3)$. Using
$p(a,b) = p(a \bigm | b) p(b)$, we can also write the probability of the
$x$ variables conditioned on the observations $y$,
$$p(x_1, x_2, x_3 \bigm | y_1, y_2, y_3) =  
\frac{1}{p(\mathbf{y})} \phi_{12}(x_1, x_2)  \phi_{23}(x_2, x_3) \psi_{1}(y_1, x_1) \psi_{2}(y_2, x_2) \psi_{3}(y_3, x_3).$$
For brevity, we write $p(\mathbf{y})$ for $p(y_1, y_2, y_3)$. Thus, to
form the conditional distribution, within a normalization factor, we
simply include the observed variable values into the joint probability.
For vision applications, we often use such Markov chain structures to
describe events over time.

To capture relationships over space, a two-dimensional (2D) structure is
useful, called a **Markov random field** (MRF) @Blake2011:

![Two-dimensional Markov random field.](figures/graphical_models/mrf.png){width="48%" #fig-leafs}

Then the joint probability over all the variables factorizes into this
product: 

$$p(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{y}) = 
\frac{1}{p(\mathbf{y})}
\prod_{(i,j)} \phi_{ij}(x_i, x_j) \prod_i \psi_i(x_i, y_i),$$
where the first product is over all spatial neighbors $i$ and $j$, and the second
product is over all nodes $i$.

An example of how Markov random field models are applied to images is
depicted in @fig-leafs, which show a small image region and its context
in the image (@fig-leafs [a]). @fig-leafs [b] shows an MRF with each
node corresponding to a pixel of the image region. The states of an MRF
can be indicator variables of image segment membership for each pixel.
The states of a hypothetical most-probable configuration of this MRF are
shown as the color of each node in this illustration.

:::{#fig-leafs layout-ncol="2"}
![](figures/graphical_models/leaf2.jpg){width=97% #fig-leafs-a}

![](figures/graphical_models/leaf1.jpg){width=100% #fig-leafs-b}

Fig (a) Image to be segmented and a local region of (a) marked in red.  (b) Visualization of an MRF of nodes corresponding to image pixels inside the marked region, with states indicating segment membership, for a hypothetical most probable configuration.
::: 

## Directed Graphical Models

In addition to undirected graphical models, another type of graphical
model is commonly used. **Directed graphical models** @Koller2009
describe factorizations of the joint probability into products of
conditional probability distributions. Each node in a directed graph
contributes a well-specified factor in the joint probability: the
probability of its variable, conditioned on all the variables originating
arrows pointing into it. So this graph

![A directed graphical model with three variables.](figures/graphical_models/directed.png){width="20%" #eq-directedjoint}

denotes the joint probability,

elements: 3x3 latent grid nodes (x_ij, represented as spheres initially white)
3x3 observed nodes (y_ij, represented as spheres positioned vertically above x_ij)
Vertical line segments connecting each x_ij to its corresponding y_ij
Horizontal grid lines connecting adjacent x_ij nodes along the row direction
Depth grid lines connecting adjacent x_ij nodes along the column direction
Extended boundary lines on the right and front edges of the x-grid to indicate an infinite/larger MRF
Text labels for the back-row nodes: x_1, x_2, x_3 and y_1, y_2, y_3

interactions.label: Spatial coupling (phi)
interactions.teaches: Higher coupling forces neighboring hidden states to agree, smoothing out local noise in the observations.

interactions.label: Toggle Observation State
interactions.teaches: Clicking any top-layer observation node 'y' toggles its state (color), triggering real-time inference that propagates to the hidden 'x' nodes.

demo_steps.title: The MRF Structure
demo_steps.narration: In this 2D Markov Random Field, the bottom layer contains the hidden states (x, white), and the top layer contains our noisy observations (y, grey). Vertical edges represent local evidence (unary potentials), while the grid lines represent spatial interactions (pairwise potentials).

demo_steps.title: Independent Decisions (No Coupling)
demo_steps.narration: With spatial coupling set to 0, each hidden node 'x' is determined entirely by its own observation 'y'. If the observations are noisy (mixed colors), the estimated hidden state is equally noisy and lacks spatial coherence.

demo_steps.title: Enforcing Spatial Consistency
demo_steps.narration: Increase the coupling parameter. Now, neighboring hidden nodes penalize sudden changes. The grid performs joint inference: isolated noisy observations are smoothed out, forcing the hidden layer to form clean, continuous segments.

demo_steps.title: Interactive Belief Propagation
demo_steps.narration: Try clicking on any of the top-layer observation nodes (y) to change their values. Watch how the change dynamically propagates to its neighbors in the hidden layer (x) based on the coupling strength.

interactionPlan.camera_suggestion: An orthographic view from a slightly elevated, angled perspective looking down at the 3x3 grid, showing clear separation between the top (y) and bottom (x) layers.
interactionPlan.view_reasoning: (1) The dominant vertical lines linking x and y run straight up-and-down on the screen. The grid plane of x nodes lies flat, with grid lines running left-right and receding diagonally into the background. (2) This receding diagonal depth implies the camera is rotated around the vertical Y-axis by about -35 degrees (azimuth) to reveal the 2D grid structure clearly without alignment overlap. (3) The vertical separation between the two layers is highly visible, meaning the elevation must be high enough to see the grid rows but shallow enough to emphasize the vertical vertical edges, indicating an elevation of about 25 degrees.

camera_view.view_notes: Maintains the classic oblique textbook perspective of the graphical model where nodes align nicely along diagonal grid axes.

inline_constraints.default_view: Must match the original node positioning, horizontal layout, and vertical projection.
inline_constraints.visible_ui: A single compact slider for spatial coupling placed near the bottom edge.
inline_constraints.explainers: Clicking a top node shows a hover tooltip: 'Observed State (Click to toggle)'.
inline_constraints.framing: Keep a moderate margin around the grid to prevent boundary lines from being clipped.
inline_constraints.camera: Match the visual proportions of the original diagram exactly on first load.

interactionPlan.notes: Represent node states using distinct colors (e.g., Purple and Green representing two classes in binary segmentation). When the user toggles a 'y' node or adjusts the slider, run a quick iterative energy minimization (or basic belief propagation) step on a 3x3 MRF to update the colors of the 'x' nodes instantly. Render connection lines as simple cylinder/line elements.

evaluation.geometry_accuracy_analysis: The 3D grid layout, spheres, cylinder connectors, and boundary extensions are fully represented using real 3D primitives. However, the camera's default viewpoint features a significant roll angle (29 degrees) that tilts the entire grid diagonally, failing to match the horizontal alignment of the source figure and making the spatial relationships harder to parse.
evaluation.geometry_accuracy_improvement: Adjust the default camera settings to eliminate the roll angle (set rollDeg to 0) and modify the azimuth/elevation to align the grid lines with the perspective layout of the original source image.
evaluation.interactivity_usability_analysis: The developer implemented three high-quality, functional interactions: (1) A 'Spatial coupling (phi)' slider that dynamically updates the pairwise coupling parameter. (2) Interactive 3D click events on each observation node 'y_i' which toggle their binary state and trigger a real-time exact MAP inference (energy minimization) algorithm to update the hidden 'x_i' nodes. (3) A 'toggle y' button to toggle the selected node. (4) A guided step-through sequence containing 4 detailed steps, which is wired to both the global window object and an in-scene click handler on the grid lines.
evaluation.faithfulness_analysis: The basic topology of the grid and the color scheme of white and grey nodes match the source figure. However, the camera angle is highly tilted, causing the vertical connections to appear skewed rather than straight up. Additionally, the text labels (x and y) severely overlap with the node geometries, making them hard to read.
discrepancies: Vertical connections from white to grey nodes are slanted instead of perpendicular to the grid.
Text labels (x1, x2, x3, y1, y2, y3) overlap directly with the node spheres instead of being clearly offset above them.
The overall perspective projection is rotated and lacks the clean orthographic look of the source diagram.
evaluation.faithfulness_improvement: Adjust the label offsets to prevent overlapping with the nodes, and align the camera view and node heights so the vertical connections are perfectly upright.
evaluation.label_quality_analysis: Source labels include x1, x2, x3 for the white nodes and y1, y2, y3 for the gray observed nodes. In the output, all six labels are present, but their placement is highly problematic. Specifically, y2 and y3 directly overlap the node spheres, and x2 and x3 are poorly positioned relative to their target nodes, causing legibility issues.
evaluation.label_quality_improvement: Adjust the 3D position offsets for the y2, y3, and x series labels so they hover clearly above or beside their respective spheres without intersecting the geometry.
evaluation.concept_accuracy_analysis: Core concepts: 2D Markov Random Fields, spatial coupling (pairwise potentials), and joint inference (MAP estimation). User-visible claims and features: (1) Nodes $x_i$ and $y_i$ are accurately labeled and positioned in two distinct layers. (2) The coupling slider dynamically modifies the pairwise strength parameter, correctly demonstrating how independent local evidence gives way to spatial coherence. (3) Toggling observation nodes computes a mathematically exact MAP estimate over the 512 state combinations of the 3x3 grid in real-time, showing accurate spatial propagation and smoothing of noise. All interactive behaviors and descriptions are conceptually flawless.
evaluation.notes: While the interactive MAP inference engine and MRF concept demonstration are exceptionally strong, the visual presentation is severely marred by a highly tilted camera roll and overlapping labels. The camera's diagonal tilt makes the vertical lines appear skewed rather than straight up, and several node labels clash directly with the sphere geometries.
action_items: Fix the camera view parameters: set rollDeg to 0, and adjust azimuthDeg and elevationDeg so the grid aligns with the source perspective, making the vertical links appear upright and parallel.
Adjust the 3D offset positions for labels x1, x2, x3, y1, y2, and y3 to prevent them from overlapping with the sphere geometries and ensure clear legibility.
Increase the vertical spacing (obsHeight) or adjust label positions so that the labels of the back row do not clash with the spheres in front of them.
